text: {"answer": "Divalent cations like Ca2+ are far more effective than monovalent ions at compressing the electrical double layer and neutralizing the negative surface charge on plastic particles, which reduces electrostatic repulsion and lowers the energy barrier against aggregation (PMC11899741:L77; PMC13213765:L44; PMC11543686:L90). This is because the critical coagulation concentration is inversely proportional to the sixth power of ionic charge (Schulze-Hardy rule), making divalent ions roughly 50–83 times more effective at inducing particle coalescence than monovalent ions (PMC12376886:L46). Mechanistically, divalent cations such as Ca2+ also produce a stronger charge-screening effect than monovalent ions like Na+ at the same ionic strength (PMC9142603:L95), and carboxyl or other negatively charged surface groups can bind Ca2+ more readily, promoting cation bridging between particles that further enhances aggregation/retention (PMC11899741:L77).", "citations": ["PMC11899741:L77", "PMC13213765:L44", "PMC11543686:L90", "PMC12376886:L46", "PMC9142603:L95"]}

{"answer": "A zeta potential near zero means the electrostatic repulsive forces between particles are minimal, so there is insufficient repulsion to keep particles apart (PMC10313666:L27, PMC13488408:L23). When attractive forces (e.g., van der Waals) then exceed these weak repulsive forces, the suspension becomes unstable and particles collide and stick together, i.e., aggregate or agglomerate (PMC10313666:L27, PMC11494166:L27). This zero-charge condition is often called the isoelectric point, and particles with high positive or negative zeta potential instead repel each other and resist aggregation, confirming that it is the loss of repulsion near zero that drives aggregation (PMC11494166:L27, PMC8617854:L34, PMC12003597:L64).", "citations": ["PMC10313666:L27", "PMC13488408:L23", "PMC11494166:L27", "PMC8617854:L34", "PMC12003597:L64"]}

{"answer": "Increasing ionic strength raises the concentration of counter-ions near the charged particle surface, which compresses the electrical double layer and produces electrostatic screening of the surface charge (PMC13298883:L22, PMC13298883:L36). This charge screening effect, exerted by background cations such as Na+ or Ca2+, reduces the effective surface charge detected, lowering the magnitude of the measured zeta potential (PMC9142603:L95). As a result, at higher ionic strengths the electrokinetic response and zeta potential shifts are diminished because electrostatic screening suppresses the double-layer potential that zeta potential measurements reflect (PMC13298883:L36).", "citations": ["PMC13298883:L22", "PMC13298883:L36", "PMC9142603:L95"]}

{"answer": "An eco-corona or biofilm is formed when biomolecules (proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, humic/fulvic acids, EPS, soil metabolites) adsorb onto the plastic surface via van der Waals and electrostatic interactions, creating a new outer layer with its own ionizable functional groups (e.g., carboxylic groups from humic/fulvic acids, amine/carboxyl groups from EPS) that shield or replace the native plastic surface charge, so the zeta potential measured reflects this adsorbed layer rather than the bare polymer. Because the corona components alter functional-group composition and charge distribution, they can make the particle more negative (humic/fulvic acid carboxyl groups), shield positive charges on amine-functionalized plastics and even cause charge reversal at high EPS concentrations, or leave zeta potential largely unchanged while thickness/physical properties dominate instead. Thicker or more tightly bound (hard) coronas further shield the underlying surface charge, slowing electrophoretic mobility and giving a smaller measured zeta potential.", "citations": ["PMC13394419:L25", "PMC13394419:L31", "PMC10830523:L132", "PMC10830523:L134", "PMC13057466:L53", "PMC13057466:L39", "PMC4958399:L42"]}

{"answer": "Carboxyl groups are acidic and dissociate/deprotonate in water to leave negatively charged –COO⁻ moieties on the particle surface, whereas amine groups are basic and can protonate to give positively charged –NH3+ groups, so the two functionalizations impart opposite charge character to the surface (PMC11103427:L23, PMC10483464 context not applicable). However, in practice this theoretical positive charge for amine particles is not always observed: one study found PS-NH2 showed the most negative zeta potential of all tested particles, attributing this to solution pH being below the amine's pKa (limiting protonation), the inherent negative charge of the polystyrene core, and possible specific adsorption of anions at amine sites (PMC13104249:L42). Thus the opposite nominal charges arise from the differing acid-base chemistry of carboxyl (acidic, deprotonates to anionic) versus amine (basic, protonates to cationic) groups, though the net measured zeta potential also depends on pH and the underlying polymer core.", "citations": ["PMC13104249:L42", "PMC11103427:L23"]}

{"answer": "When proteins adsorb onto a plastic particle's surface to form a corona, they coat and shield the particle's native surface charge, altering the surface charge density that is measured as zeta potential (PMC4958399:L39, PMC4958399:L42). A hard corona layer in particular shields the negative particle surface and slows particle translocation velocity, which is read out as a smaller (less negative) zeta potential value (PMC4958399:L42). The magnitude of this shift depends on protein identity/affinity and incubation conditions—e.g., proteins with isoelectric points further from the suspension pH occupy more surface area and cause larger zeta potential changes (PMC4958399:L39)—and on corona thickness/density, since more bound protein coverage reduces translocation velocity and thus reduces the measured zeta potential, while loss of loosely bound soft corona proteins increases it again (PMC4958399:L49). Separately, protein adsorption can also affect zeta potential through changes in particle size/corona thickness in biological media (PMC13241894:L79, PMC13258071:L39)."}

{"answer": "Natural organic matter (e.g., humic/fulvic acids, EPS) adsorbs onto the particle surface, forming an eco-corona/adsorbed layer that introduces its own charged functional groups (notably carboxylic groups, which are negatively charged) onto the particle, thereby shifting the measured zeta potential toward more negative values. This adsorption is not always uniform—NOM molecules can attach as discrete 'patches,' creating localized charge heterogeneities on an otherwise oppositely charged surface, which changes electrostatic behavior even without full charge reversal. In some cases NOM coatings also add steric/negative charge shielding that offsets charge from other adsorbed species (e.g., iron oxides), further altering the net measured surface charge.", "citations": ["PMC10830523:L132", "PMC13057466:L62", "PMC7918465:L21", "PMC13213765:L56"]}

{"answer": "UV weathering breaks polymer chains via photo-oxidation (Norrish Type I reactions) and creates microcracks, surface roughness, and increased porosity on the plastic surface (PMC8038232:L19; PMC11851392:L80). This process generates oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carbonyl and hydroxyl groups) at the particle surface, which increases polarity and hydrophilicity (PMC8038232:L34; PMC12030786:L119). These additional surface oxygen functional groups and greater surface density of acidic/polar groups increase surface charge, making the zeta potential more negative under neutral and alkaline conditions compared to pristine, non-weathered particles (PMC8038232:L34; PMC12030786:L119).", "citations": ["PMC8038232:L34", "PMC8038232:L19", "PMC11851392:L80", "PMC12030786:L119"]}

{"answer": "Surfactants and dispersants adsorb directly onto the particle surface, so the zeta potential measured is not the bare polymer's charge but the charge of this adsorbed layer at the particle–liquid interface (PMC10734291:L62, PMC12637955:L12). For ionic surfactants like CTAB, as more surfactant adsorbs the surface charge evolves toward the surfactant's own head-group charge, even causing charge inversion from negative to positive, while nonionic surfactants such as Tween 20 instead lower the absolute magnitude of the zeta potential by masking/shielding the underlying charge (PMC10734291:L62; PMC8719689:L36). Dissolved ions/electrolytes in the dispersant also adsorb as counter-ions and compress the electrical double layer around the particle, further altering the measured potential (PMC8719689:L36; PMC13488408:L73). Because zeta potential is thus dependent on the specific dispersant/medium used, measurements in different media (e.g., water vs. cell culture medium with serum, where a protein corona forms) give different zeta potential values for the same particle (PMC12590796:L66; PMC12590796:L72).", "citations": ["PMC10734291:L62", "PMC8719689:L36", "PMC13488408:L73", "PMC12637955:L12", "PMC12590796:L66", "PMC12590796:L72"]}
